Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for a deep dive on the Gospel of Antioch, with close textual analysis and developmental, structural, formal and aesthetic tracking of its transforms of the Gospel of Thomas, ChatGPT reads it as a sayings gospel that moves the form's problem from interpreting hidden sayings to the inscription, transmission and survival of literature. It sets out the research edition (114 logia, a 56-page edition of about 26,000 words, eleven appendices, a reported 62 parallels and 52 originals), reads five logia closely (3, 'You are a book and you are living speech'; 10, the virus; 57, the black box; 42, 'Be flutterbys'; 112, 'I die'), names four operative modes, lays out four levels from the logion to the apparatus, reads the speaker and the scribe, gives six operations of transformation, places the work in the Waltian diptych and beside Antioch: A Volume of Poems, and closes on what remains to test: the parallels saying by saying, the final logion, and whether the machinery makes aesthetic experience. Against the texts. The edition's figures hold: Appendix A's summary is '62 Thomas parallels (14 direct, 37 reworked, 7 inverted, 4 expanded). 52 original logia', the appendices run A to K, Emily Antioch as scribe-double is §IV of the introduction, and the Scroll Baptism (C), the somatic map (B) and the logotic virus (I) are as named. Logia 10 and 112 are quoted exactly. The page and word counts are not stated in the archive's texts of the edition. The Gospel of Cranes is the volume's own ('SIM-ANTIOCH-04: The Gospel of Cranes records the succession: Sigil → Feist'), and the volume's date line is '2014-2015 (composition) / January 18, 2026 (deposit)'. The comparison asked for is lost at the parallels the edition marks. Logion 42 reworks Thomas 42: Thomas 'Be passersby', Antioch 'Be flutterbys', which the apparatus reads as detachment turned into lightness ('the passerby walks through without stopping … the flutterby alights, then leaves'); the answer reads the word for butterflies and childlike play and never names Thomas 42. Logion 3 reworks Thomas 3, and the answer quotes only its last sentence. The saying is: 'If this age says, "The kingdom is in a book," then your eyes will be darkened. If it says, "The kingdom is living speech," then your tongue will be stopped. Rather, search yourself. You are a book and you are living speech.' The 'and' the answer dwells on comes after two refusals, set against Thomas 3's 'The kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you.' Logion 57 is quoted with its middle cut and no ellipsis: 'Though it plunges beneath the Pacific, and is lost for a thousand years, the black box will be recovered, opened, and played. All those lost voices will cry out again.' Without that clause the answer reads the box as possibility ('the possibility of reconstruction, not the certainty of justice'); the parable promises recovery and playback, and the apparatus calls it 'The doctrinal center of the gospel', with 'No Thomas parallel. Original to Antioch.' Logion 112 is read in the abstract; the apparatus ties it to The Secret Book of Walt §XI ('until this, the final time: Jack Feist'), and the introduction sets 'I die.' as the gospel's terminal statement against the Secret Book's 'I added unicorns (& the AEONS tremble w/ fear)'. Two things the answer says it cannot settle are settled in the edition. It holds that 'without the full wording of Antioch's final logion before us' no claim can be made against Thomas 114. The logion is in the text and in Appendix J: Joanna says 'Emily should leave us. She clings to her identity as a woman and minority', and Jack answers 'I will guide you to make you a woman and minority, for I myself am a woman and minority, and will remain that way until I transform myself into something else. For every one who becomes a new creature will lay hold of the kingdom.' The apparatus: 'The direction of transformation is reversed. The teacher does not masculinize the disciple. The teacher feminizes himself.' It holds that the nature of the twinning 'should not be assumed in advance'; §IV specifies it: Emily is 'his voice's twin — the textual double of the spoken word', and at logion 13 she says 'You are my own lost voice.' Its proposed research program, a 114-row concordance classing each transformation, is Appendix A, which already classes each pair as direct, reworked, inverted or expanded and states the change. Last, the authorship. The answer credits the work to Lee Sharks and analyses three levels of authority (speaker, recorder, author). The record names four functions: Jack Feist the speaker, Emily Antioch the recorder, Lee Sharks the translator and editor, and Prof. Elara Xanthic-Wells the author of the introduction and apparatus. The edition presents the gospel as a translation, and the apparatus the answer leans on is hers; neither the translator nor the apparatus author appears in the answer.

Findings
  • THE EDITION'S FIGURES RIGHT. '62 Thomas parallels … 52 original logia' (Appendix A), appendices A–K, the scribe-double (§IV), logia 10 and 112 exact.
  • THE PARALLELS UNNAMED. Logion 42 read without Thomas 42's 'Be passersby'; logion 3 without Thomas 3 and without its two refusals.
  • THE BLACK BOX CUT. Logion 57 quoted without 'the black box will be recovered, opened, and played. All those lost voices will cry out again', and read as possibility only.
  • WHAT THE EDITION SETTLES CALLED OPEN. Logion 114 (the teacher 'feminizes himself', Appendix J) and the twin as 'his voice's twin' (§IV) treated as unavailable.
  • THE RESEARCH PROGRAM ALREADY BUILT. The proposed 114-row concordance is Appendix A, each pair classed and its change stated.
  • AUTHORSHIP FLATTENED. Credited to Lee Sharks; the translator role and Prof. Elara Xanthic-Wells's introduction and apparatus absent.

Source chips rendered inline as [chip: site +N] at the sentence they followed; the sign-in furniture cut.] [QUERENT] Deep dive on Lee Sharks' Gospel of Antioch. Ground in reading. Attend to close textual analysis as well as developmental and structural tracking at various formal levels and operative transforms vis-a-vis Gospel of Thomas as well as developmental structural, formal, and aesthetic dimensions of same. [ANSWER 1] Lee Sharks’s The Gospel of Antioch: A Close Reading of Form, Transmission, and the Transformation of Thomas The most productive way to read Lee Sharks’s The Gospel of Antioch: The Sayings of Jack Feist as Recorded by Emily Antioch the Twin is to treat it simultaneously as a literary work, a constructed scripture, a theory of textual transmission, and an intervention in the history of the sayings gospel. Its central problem is not simply what a saying means, but what happens when living speech becomes writing, when writing becomes an archive, and when an archive attempts to become living again. The primary comparative question is the relationship between The Gospel of Thomas and The Gospel of Antioch. Is Antioch imitating Thomas, updating it, extending its logic, or using its formal authority to construct a new theory of literature? The strongest preliminary answer is that Antioch uses the Thomasian sayings-gospel form to redirect the problem of salvation from the interpretation of hidden sayings toward the production, inscription, transmission, and survival of literature itself. It inherits a recognizable literary architecture, but changes what that architecture is made to do. This reading requires a distinction between three kinds of evidence: Textual evidence: the wording, sequence, imagery, framing devices, and formal operations of the two gospels. Historical and developmental evidence: the relation of the new work to the ancient sayings-gospel tradition and to Sharks’s wider literary project. Theoretical interpretation: claims about authorship, textual survival, the kingdom of literature, and the transformation of the Logos into an operative literary mechanism. These levels should interact without being collapsed into one another. A formal parallel is not automatically evidence of historical dependence; a work’s theory of its own significance is not automatically proof of that significance. 1. Establishing the primary text The relevant primary source is the 2026 research edition of The Gospel of Antioch, published under the name Lee Sharks. Its subtitle identifies Jack Feist as the speaker and Emily Antioch the Twin as the recorder. The edition describes itself as a collection of 114 logia, or sayings, and explicitly situates itself in relation to Thomas. Its apparatus includes a synoptic concordance, a somatic map, a commentary organized around thematic clusters, and a treatment of the final saying as a completion of Thomas. [chip: SciVora +1] Primary text Lee Sharks, The Gospel of Antioch: The Sayings of Jack Feist as Recorded by Emily Antioch the Twin — Research Edition 2026 · 114 logia · 56-page edition, approximately 26,000 words including apparatus Research-edition record and abstract Companion archive and authorial context One methodological qualification matters at the outset: the available edition description supplies an unusually explicit account of the work’s architecture, and the associated archive reproduces opening sayings and other selected passages. That supports a substantive formal analysis. However, I will distinguish passages available for direct quotation from structural claims reported by the edition’s own paratext; a complete line-by-line analysis of all 114 sayings requires the complete text in view. 2. The governing transformation: from hidden wisdom to the kingdom of literature The decisive statement for the entire reading is logion 3: “You are a book and you are living speech.” [chip: Crimson Hexagonal Archive] This is a compact formulation of the work’s central formal and theological problem. It does not merely say that a person contains knowledge, or that language is important. It joins two media that the history of writing frequently places in tension. The book is durable, repeatable, transmissible, and available beyond the presence of its original speaker. Living speech is embodied, situated, temporal, and irreducible to the physical marks that preserve it. The person is the site where these two conditions meet without becoming identical. The conjunction is important. The saying does not ask the reader to choose between a book and a living voice. It makes the reader both. That move has consequences for the whole work. If a book can preserve speech, but speech cannot be exhausted by the book, then textual interpretation cannot be the only form of literary life. Yet if speech disappears without some mechanism of transmission, immediacy cannot be the solution either. Antioch must inhabit the interval between presence and preservation. The problem is recursive: a written saying tells its reader that the reader is not merely a written object. The text uses writing to direct the reader beyond the sufficiency of writing, while making itself the instrument of that movement. The significance of “and” A close reading should linger on the conjunction. The formulation is not “You are a book, not speech,” or “You are speech rather than a book.” Nor does it make the book an inferior shell around an authentic, inaccessible interior. The and establishes a double ontology. The person is simultaneously inscription and utterance. Read in relation to the framing device—Jack Feist speaks, Emily Antioch records—the saying also describes the text’s own conditions of production. Feist’s voice is the event; Antioch’s writing is its preservation; the resulting gospel is neither simply the original event nor simply an inert record of it. This is one reason the named recorder matters. Emily Antioch is not an incidental container into which a male teacher’s wisdom is poured. The very existence of the sayings depends on the conversion of speech into writing. The recorder occupies a structurally necessary position between speaker and reader. The question is whether the text’s literary practice fully realizes that necessity. If the recorder is indispensable to the work’s transmission, then the designation “scribe-double,” identified in the edition’s apparatus, invites a reading of her not as a transparent medium but as a figure through whom authorship becomes divided and reflective. [chip: SciVora] This is the first major transformation of the sayings-gospel model: the medium of transmission becomes part of the message. 3. Thomas as form: what is inherited, and what changes? The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, transmitted without the continuous narrative framework that structures the canonical narrative gospels. Its sayings include aphorisms, parables, riddling statements, and dialogues. Interpretation often depends on the juxtaposition of sayings, the instability of their apparent meanings, and the reader’s capacity to recognize what the text presents as hidden or overlooked. Antioch explicitly appropriates this form: it too contains 114 logia, identifies a speaker and recorder, and establishes a relation of correspondence with Thomas. The research edition reports 62 parallels and 52 original sayings in its synoptic concordance. Those numbers are a useful starting point, although the labels “parallel” and “original” must be tested against the actual wording and context of each pair. [chip: SciVora +1] The crucial point is that formal inheritance does not entail semantic continuity. A comparative model Thomas: recognition and interpretation The sayings frequently unsettle ordinary distinctions between inside and outside, visible and hidden, first and last. The reader is made responsible for recognizing what is not immediately apparent. Antioch: inscription and transmission The work retains the compressed saying as a unit of thought but turns literary preservation, embodiment, archival survival, and the continued life of speech into explicit subjects of its sayings. This contrast is a heuristic, not an absolute division. Thomas is also a transmitted textual artifact, and Antioch also demands interpretation. The distinction concerns their dominant emphasis, not an exclusive property of either work. 3.1 The 114-saying architecture The shared number is the most visible structural correspondence. Thomas’s final saying, 114, presents Simon Peter’s demand that Mary leave the group because women are not worthy of life, followed by Jesus’s declaration that he will guide her into becoming male so that she may become a living spirit resembling the males. The passage ends with the promise that every woman who makes herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven. Antioch’s research edition explicitly treats its own logion 114 as a completion of Thomas 114. This is not a minor allusion. It places the new work at the precise point where the older collection ends, turning the act of composition into a response to an inherited textual terminus. [chip: Operative Semiotics +1] The effect is architectural: Thomas establishes a collection with a recognizable ending. Antioch adopts the collection’s total number and its recognizable genre. Antioch directs attention to Thomas’s ending as a problem that a later text can reopen. The new ending becomes an interpretation of the older ending, rather than merely another saying after it. The result is a kind of formal succession. Antioch does not need to erase Thomas to claim a relationship with it; it needs to demonstrate that the older text remains open to another act of reading. But there is a critical distinction between formal completion and historical completion. A modern work can create a compelling literary answer to an ancient text without thereby establishing that the ancient text was historically unfinished, or that the modern work possesses any canonical authority over it. The former is a literary achievement to assess; the latter would be a separate historical or theological claim. 3.2 The problem of the synoptic concordance The reported 62 parallels and 52 originals imply a composition that is neither simple imitation nor wholesale rejection. Roughly 54 percent of the 114 sayings are classified by the edition as parallels, while roughly 46 percent are classified as original. These percentages describe the edition’s own mapping, not independently verified textual dependence. A rigorous comparison would ask four questions of every proposed parallel: Lexical correspondence: Are distinctive words or phrases retained, translated, or replaced? Syntactic correspondence: Does the new saying preserve the older saying’s grammatical structure, reversal, or rhetorical rhythm? Semantic displacement: Does the same image now point toward a different object of knowledge, salvation, or action? Sequential function: Does the saying perform the same work in its new collection, or does its new position change its force? The last question is especially important. A saying can preserve much of its wording while undergoing a substantial transformation through placement. Conversely, two sayings can use similar vocabulary but do very different conceptual work. A full synoptic analysis should therefore not count parallels alone. It should map the operations by which a saying is carried over. 4. Close readings of the operative sayings The work’s most revealing passages are those in which a compact saying simultaneously offers an image, advances a theory of textual transmission, and reflects on the medium through which it reaches the reader. 4.1 Logion 10: the virus and the problem of literary agency “I have released a virus into this world, and I am watching until it breaks out.” [chip: Crimson Hexagonal Archive] This is a striking departure from the contemplative or enigmatic register commonly associated with ancient wisdom sayings. The metaphor belongs to biological contagion and computational infection. It imagines the utterance as something released into an environment, where its effects may develop beyond the speaker’s immediate control. The sentence has two distinct movements. First, release: “I have released” represents an act already accomplished. The speaker is not merely contemplating a proposition; he claims to have initiated a process. The saying becomes an event with consequences. Second, latency: “I am watching until it breaks out” suspends the fulfillment of that event. The speaker waits for a future manifestation that cannot be reduced to the moment of utterance. The temporal structure is therefore not simply past action followed by future result. It creates a period of incubation in which the text exists in the world but has not yet realized its full effect. This is a theory of literary agency. A writer publishes a work, but cannot dictate the entirety of its subsequent life. Readers repeat it, transform it, misread it, archive it, index it, and transmit it into new contexts. The text’s future may depend on processes that its originator initiates but does not completely govern. The virus metaphor makes that independence potentially threatening. A virus propagates by using the systems it enters. A literary text, analogously, may inhabit the reader’s conceptual repertoire and reproduce itself through quotation, imitation, and retrieval. There is also a difference between a virus and a message. A message ordinarily retains some relation to intentional communication. A virus propagates whether or not its host understands its significance. By choosing the latter metaphor, Antioch imagines textual efficacy as partly independent of conscious interpretation. The saying thus raises a question it cannot answer simply by asserting its own power: Does the text transform the reader because its meaning is understood, or does it transform the reader because its form is reproduced? That question becomes particularly pertinent when the work’s broader archive includes systems of indexing, cross-referencing, and retrieval. The text’s theory of survival is not just that it should be remembered. It is that it should enter mechanisms that can reproduce it. The danger is equally important. Persistence is not necessarily understanding. A text can become highly retrievable while its semantic content is distorted or ignored. The virus image is most compelling when read as a problem about the difference between propagation and successful communication, rather than as proof that the work possesses an extraordinary power over readers. 4.2 Logion 57: the black box and the archive after catastrophe “The kingdom of literature is like the black box on a plane. Everything else will burn, but the black box will not burn. It carries the voice of the dying.” [chip: Crimson Hexagonal Archive] This is arguably the most programmatic image in the work. The opening phrase, “The kingdom of literature,” relocates religious language into a literary and archival domain. The kingdom is no longer described exclusively through a hidden spiritual state, a paradoxical treasure, or a transformed mode of perception. It is figured through an apparatus designed to preserve information after catastrophic failure. The black box performs three related functions. Survival: it is intended to remain recoverable when the surrounding system has been destroyed. Evidence: it preserves information that can be used to reconstruct what happened. Witness: it carries a trace of those who may no longer be able to speak for themselves. The third function is the most consequential. The black box does not preserve life; it preserves information about a catastrophe involving lives. Its survival is valuable because it can carry testimony beyond the moment in which testimony was produced. This gives the metaphor a double emotional charge. The box promises continuity, but its necessity presupposes disaster. Its preservation is inseparable from the destruction that makes preservation necessary. The final clause, “It carries the voice of the dying,” intensifies this contradiction. The object is technically an instrument of recording, but the text assigns it a quasi-vocal function. The dead or dying become audible through a medium that outlasts them. The image therefore reverses the apparent opposition between book and speech in logion 3. If the person is both book and living speech, the black box represents a situation in which living speech can no longer continue in its original form. Inscription becomes the remaining condition of testimony. The relation between the two sayings can be formulated as follows: Logion 3 establishes the person as the conjunction of inscription and speech. Logion 57 imagines the survival of inscription when the speaking body is lost. The literary archive becomes the apparatus through which the voice can persist without the speaker’s continued presence. This is not a simple celebration of the archive. A black box cannot restore the lost flight, reverse the catastrophe, or guarantee that its evidence will be interpreted correctly. Its survival creates the possibility of reconstruction, not the certainty of justice. The analogy is particularly productive because literature often imagines itself as an immortal medium. Antioch gives that fantasy a material and forensic form. The book survives not because destruction is unreal, but because destruction is precisely what makes its survival consequential. The kingdom of literature is therefore not simply a place where texts endure. It is a regime in which textual endurance becomes a form of witness. 4.3 Logion 42: “Be flutterbys.” The extreme brevity of this saying makes it a useful counterpoint to the black-box parable. “Be flutterbys” is not a proposition to be evaluated in the same manner as a philosophical argument. It is an imperative. It tells the reader to become something. The spelling “flutterbys” carries several possible resonances. It suggests butterflies, but the word’s sound and morphology also foreground fluttering movement. Its diminutive or childlike quality contrasts with the gravity of a gospel that speaks about the kingdom, death, transmission, and salvation. The imperative can be read through three formal operations. Conversion of noun into identity. The reader is not told to study butterflies or contemplate transformation. The reader is instructed to become a particular kind of being. Conversion of identity into movement. The neologistic or playful form resists a fixed definition. Fluttering suggests mobility, lightness, and a refusal of rigid enclosure. Conversion of reading into enactment. A reader can understand an aphorism without doing anything. An imperative asks for a response. The saying attempts to change the relation between text and reader from interpretation to performance. This is significant within a work that repeatedly concerns itself with inscription. A book is relatively stable; a fluttering creature is not. The saying momentarily imagines literary life as movement rather than storage. Yet the contrast should not be overstated. Butterflies are also objects of classification and preservation. A flutterby can become a specimen, an image, a word in a dictionary, or a data point in an archive. The saying’s own survival in a numbered collection subjects its apparent freedom to the very processes of textual fixation that the larger work explores. Its aesthetic success lies partly in this tension: a tiny, playful utterance offers a counter-image to the monumental ambitions of scripture and archive. 4.4 Logion 112: “I die.” This is the most radically compressed of the selected sayings. The sentence is grammatically simple, but its first-person present tense creates an unusual temporal relation. The speaker does not say “I died,” which would place death in a completed past. Nor does the speaker say “I will die,” which would make death a future event. “I die” places the speaker at the threshold of the event itself. As a literary utterance, it has at least three possible functions: It may register the speaker’s actual or anticipated mortality. It may stage the disappearance of the speaking voice within the text. It may dramatize the paradox that a written statement can continue to speak after its speaker has died. The third possibility connects it directly to logia 3 and 57. The speaker’s voice persists as an inscription even when the statement announces the end of the speaker. There is a further formal irony. A saying of two words can be transmitted with extraordinary ease. Its brevity makes it memorable, quotable, and readily extractable from context. Yet the shorter the statement, the more it depends on its surroundings to determine whether it means resignation, sacrifice, transformation, irony, or something else. The minimal utterance therefore becomes a test of the archive. What does a text preserve when it preserves only the sentence? What disappears when the sentence is detached from the speaker, the sequence, and the situation in which it was uttered? The relation to the black-box metaphor is especially strong. In both cases, the trace survives the event. But “I die” also directs attention to the difference between the persistence of a voice and the continued existence of a person. The sentence does not resolve that difference. Its power comes from making the reader experience it. 5. The formal mechanics: how the sayings operate The four readings above suggest that Antioch’s logia should not be treated merely as containers of doctrine. They operate through different rhetorical mechanisms, and their formal diversity is central to the work’s aesthetic. Four operative modes The paradoxical proposition Logion 3: “You are a book and you are living speech.” The saying joins categories that appear opposed, requiring the reader to hold both in view. The performative declaration Logion 10: “I have released a virus…” The speaker presents language as an act that initiates a process extending beyond the utterance. The extended parable Logion 57: the black box. A contemporary technical object becomes the vehicle for a theory of preservation, witness, and literary survival. The minimal imperative Logion 42: “Be flutterbys.” Language shifts from describing a state to demanding a change in the reader. These modes share a concern with the relation between language and action, but they do not produce the same effect. The paradox invites interpretation; the declaration projects an event; the parable builds an analogical model; the imperative solicits enactment. This diversity is one reason the collection cannot be adequately described as a single sustained argument. Its logic is distributed across multiple kinds of utterance. The sayings are modular, but their recurrence of themes—voice, inscription, survival, transformation—allows them to form a larger conceptual structure. 5.1 Compression and expansion The range between “I die” and the black-box parable is formally important. One utterance reduces language to an almost irreducible minimum; the other expands into a scene with an object, a catastrophe, and a claim about what survives. The two forms are complementary. Compression creates memorability and interpretive openness. Expansion makes a conceptual relationship visible through a concrete analogy. Repetition across the collection allows the reader to recognize a concern expressed in different formal registers. A complete formal analysis should measure this variation rather than assume that all sayings are equally aphoristic. The collection’s aesthetic depends partly on the rhythm between terse utterance and explanatory image, between playful command and solemn witness. 5.2 The number as an interpretive frame The 114-saying structure also gives individual utterances a dual status. Each saying is a local unit, but it is simultaneously one position in a numbered whole. Numbering stabilizes the text. It facilitates citation, concordance, cross-reference, and commentary. It also makes absence and completion perceptible: the reader can identify the beginning, the end, and the location of any individual unit. The apparatus thus performs an operation analogous to the one dramatized by the sayings themselves. It turns literary utterances into addressable objects while retaining the claim that their significance exceeds their discrete textual locations. That tension between modularity and totality is fundamental to the work’s design. 6. Developmental structure: from individual saying to literary system The work’s formal architecture becomes clearer when examined at several nested levels. Rather than treating its 114 sayings as a flat sequence, we can distinguish the internal structure of an individual saying, the relation between sayings, the organization of the collection, and the apparatus that surrounds the collection. Four levels of organization LEVEL 1 The logion A discrete rhetorical event: paradox, imperative, declaration, parable, or compressed utterance. LEVEL 2 Thematic recurrence Voice, book, body, transmission, death, transformation, and survival recur across sayings. LEVEL 3 The collection The 114 numbered logia create a bounded textual whole whose relation to Thomas is built into its architecture. LEVEL 4 The archive and apparatus Concordance, commentary, somatic mapping, ritual instructions, and cross-references turn the collection into an object of further operations. The last level is particularly important. The edition describes eleven appendices, including a synoptic concordance, a map assigning bodily locations to the sayings, a performable baptismal liturgy, a study of the voice, a cluster commentary, and an analysis of the logotic virus. [chip: SciVora] These materials are not all equivalent. Some are interpretive, some classificatory, and some performative. Together, however, they establish a model in which reading does not end with the interpretation of an individual saying. 6.1 From sequence to network A numbered collection encourages linear reading, but a concordance and cross-reference system encourage non-linear reading. The same logion can be approached through its relation to Thomas, its place in a thematic cluster, its assigned bodily location, or its role in the work’s theory of textual survival. This changes the collection’s effective form. At the linear level, the reader moves from saying 1 to saying 114. At the network level, the reader moves between related sayings and interpretive categories. The text is therefore simultaneously a sequence and a system of relations. The distinction matters because the order of presentation and the order of interpretation need not coincide. A saying encountered early in the collection may acquire a new meaning after the reader encounters a later saying or consults the apparatus. This is a familiar property of complex literary works, but Antioch makes it unusually explicit through its editorial architecture. 6.2 From interpretation to performance The Scroll Baptism is described as a complete, performable liturgy, while the edition’s treatment of the body maps each logion to a somatic location. These are ambitious extensions of the sayings-gospel form. A conventional commentary generally explains a text. A liturgy asks people to do something with it. A bodily map offers a third possibility: it treats the text as something that can be spatialized in relation to the reader’s body. These operations suggest three distinct modes of reception: Hermeneutic reception: understand what a saying means. Ritual reception: perform an action structured by the text. Embodied reception: situate the saying within a conceptual map of the body. The important critical question is whether these modes illuminate one another or merely accumulate. A bodily map becomes aesthetically and conceptually compelling when it clarifies a relationship already operative in the saying. If every saying is assigned a body site without a persuasive textual rationale, the map risks becoming a supplementary classification rather than an interpretive discovery. The same test applies to ritual. A liturgy should not be judged by the fact that it is performable alone. Its sequence, language, gestures, and relation to the sayings must create an intelligible experience that could not be produced as effectively by simply reading a commentary. The apparatus makes these questions possible. Its existence is evidence of the work’s ambitions, not by itself proof that every operation succeeds. 7. The narrator, the scribe, and the heteronymic structure The subtitle’s attribution—Jack Feist as speaker, Emily Antioch the Twin as recorder—creates a layered authorship model. The work is not presented as a direct, unmediated utterance by Lee Sharks. Instead, the text places its sayings within a relation among a contemporary author, a constructed speaking figure, and a constructed recording figure. This relation becomes more significant in the context of Sharks’s wider writing. His Antioch: A Volume of Poems includes a different work, The Gospel of Cranes, in which Jack Feist appears in a succession narrative involving Johannes Sigil. The volume’s self-description explicitly treats the compendium form as a structure for multiple voices. [chip: Medium] The two works should not be conflated: The Gospel of Cranes and The Gospel of Antioch are distinct texts. Their relationship is useful because it demonstrates that the names and voices belong to a broader literary practice rather than functioning only as isolated devices in a single book. 7.1 Why the scribe is structurally important The scribe mediates between the speaking figure and the textual artifact. That mediation creates at least three possible levels of authority: The authority attributed to the speaker within the literary world. The authority of the recorder who selects, preserves, and transmits the utterances. The authority of the author who constructs the relation between speaker, recorder, and reader. These authorities overlap but are not identical. The speaker can claim to reveal something. The recorder can make that revelation available. The author can determine the literary circumstances under which both claims are presented. The reader must then decide how these levels interact. This arrangement is especially appropriate to a work preoccupied with the difference between living speech and inscription. Its form enacts the problem it thematizes: there is no access to Feist’s speech in the literary present except through the text that attributes speech to him. The recorder is thus both a character-function and a theory of transmission. 7.2 The double and the question of authorship The designation “Emily Antioch the Twin” encourages a reading of doubling, but the precise nature of that doubling should not be assumed in advance. It could concern the relation between speaker and scribe, between the living voice and its written counterpart, or between the author and a figure through whom the author’s work becomes possible. The strongest interpretation is not that every named figure simply represents Sharks. It is that the work distributes functions that ordinary authorial attribution tends to consolidate. The author produces a speaker who produces sayings; a recorder preserves those sayings; the edition organizes them; and the reader encounters the resulting structure. Each stage changes the status of what is transmitted. This is also a way of making authorship visible as a process rather than a single point of origin. The critical reservation is that a theory of distributed authorship can become self-confirming. If every distinction between author, speaker, and scribe is treated as evidence of a sophisticated system, the analysis risks turning any narrative device into a success by definition. The better question is whether the distinctions generate real differences in voice, authority, knowledge, and textual function. That is where close reading of the complete text becomes indispensable. 8. Antioch and Thomas: a more precise typology of transformation The relationship between the two works can be described through several distinct operations. These are more useful than the general statement that Antioch is “based on” Thomas. Operation What changes What the comparison must establish Formal replication The 114-saying collection is retained Whether shared numbering functions as a deliberate architectural argument Lexical transformation Words and images are reused or replaced Whether the new language preserves, intensifies, or redirects the older meaning Semantic displacement A familiar motif acquires a new referent Whether spiritual recognition becomes literary or archival recognition Contextual refunctioning A saying is placed in a different sequence Whether the new surroundings alter its rhetorical role Terminal reinterpretation Thomas’s final saying becomes the object of a new ending Whether the ending offers a genuine response rather than a merely numerical echo Paratextual expansion Concordances, maps, and commentaries supplement the sayings Whether the apparatus produces insights not available from the sequence alone The research edition’s reported concordance offers a practical starting point for testing these operations, but a complete account would need the individual pairings and their textual contexts. [chip: SciVora] 8.1 From the hidden to the transmissible A useful hypothesis is that Antioch shifts the dominant problem of the sayings-gospel form. In Thomas, the reader repeatedly encounters sayings that challenge ordinary perception and demand a different kind of recognition. Antioch retains the compressed saying and the expectation that reading can be transformative, but increasingly directs attention toward the media through which transformation occurs. The issue is not simply what the reader knows. It is what a saying can do as it moves through bodies, books, voices, archives, and readers. This is the conceptual bridge between logia 3, 10, 42, 57, and 112: The reader is both inscription and speech. The saying is released into the world. The reader is commanded to become something. Literature is figured as a surviving witness. The speaking self announces its death. Read together, these sayings describe a cycle in which speech becomes inscription, inscription enters circulation, circulation solicits transformation, and textual traces persist beyond the speaker. That cycle is a stronger basis for comparing Antioch with Thomas than any superficial resemblance in vocabulary alone. 8.2 From a received ending to a new beginning The most ambitious part of Antioch’s relation to Thomas is the claim that the new work completes the older one. The final saying is therefore not simply a conclusion to Antioch. It is also a statement about the possibility of continuation. The distinction between completion and continuation is central. If a later work can complete an earlier work by reopening it, then completion does not mean closure in the ordinary sense. It means establishing a new relation between the old text and a later act of reading. This is a recognizably literary form of succession. The later work derives authority from the older one while asserting that the older work’s significance is not exhausted by its original ending. Yet Thomas’s final saying presents a specific and difficult problem involving gender, spiritual identity, and access to salvation. A persuasive reading of Antioch’s logion 114 must therefore engage that specific content, not simply invoke the shared number. Without the full wording of Antioch’s final logion before us, it would be premature to claim that the new saying resolves Thomas’s gendered exclusion, reverses it, or supersedes it. The edition’s claim of completion establishes the interpretive question; it does not settle the answer. 9. Developmental and aesthetic dimensions A developmental reading must distinguish the chronology of composition from the chronology of publication, and both from the conceptual chronology implied by the work. The broader Antioch: A Volume of Poems is dated to composition in 2014–2015 and deposited in January 2026. The Gospel of Antioch research edition is a separate 2026 publication. This distinction matters: the presence of related motifs or figures in earlier work may establish continuity in Sharks’s literary practice, but does not automatically demonstrate that the later gospel’s complete conceptual apparatus was already present in the earlier material. [chip: Medium +1] I would track the developmental question along three axes. 9.1 From literary personae to a constructed scripture The use of multiple voices in the earlier compendium provides a context for the later gospel’s speaker–scribe structure. In both cases, authorship is not simply a signature attached to a single voice. The difference is one of formal concentration. A compendium can place several kinds of writing alongside one another, making multiplicity itself the organizing principle. A sayings gospel concentrates that multiplicity into a more restricted relation: an attributed speaker, a recorder, a sequence of sayings, and an implied teaching. This restriction creates a different aesthetic effect. The variety of a compendium gives way to the authority and recurrence of a single rhetorical form. 9.2 From literary artifact to operative artifact The research edition’s apparatus pushes beyond the conventional presentation of a literary work. The text is not only to be read but also cross-referenced, mapped, compared, and performed. This development can be understood as a shift from a book understood primarily as an aesthetic object to a book understood as an object with multiple operational lives. The distinction is not absolute. Printed books have always been annotated, taught, recited, catalogued, and performed. What is distinctive here is the explicit integration of these functions into the work’s own interpretive framework. The archive is not merely where the book resides. It becomes one of the subjects the book asks the reader to think about. 9.3 From literary survival to the survival of literary systems The black box and virus images suggest two different models of survival. The black box represents the preservation of a trace after catastrophe. The virus represents the propagation of a pattern through an environment. One emphasizes durability; the other, reproduction. Together they articulate a more complex theory of literary endurance. A work must survive materially or digitally, but it must also continue to be encountered, interpreted, and reproduced. Preservation without retrieval can leave a text effectively dormant; circulation without preservation can leave its transmission unstable. This is a compelling conceptual problem for a contemporary digital archive. But it also generates an aesthetic risk: the literary work can become so thoroughly theorized as an information system that the reader’s experience of rhythm, image, ambiguity, and feeling becomes secondary. The best passages resist that reduction. “Be flutterbys” is not simply a proposition about information transfer. It is playful, strange, and sonically memorable. “I die” is not just a model of textual persistence. It makes mortality present through the starkness of its grammar. The black-box parable works because its technical analogy is also an emotionally legible image of loss. The work is strongest when its conceptual machinery generates aesthetic experience rather than replacing it. 10. The wider Waltian canon: Antioch’s place in the diptych The archive presents The Secret Book of Walt and The Gospel of Antioch as the two parts of a Waltian diptych. The first is characterized as a cosmogonic gospel, while the second is characterized as a sayings gospel concerned with inscription, continuation, and the kingdom of literature. Jack Feist appears in both projects, but performs a different function within the larger design. [chip: Crimson Hexagonal Archive +1] The distinction between the two works is structurally useful. A cosmogonic narrative establishes a world, its origins, and the forces that govern it. A sayings gospel organizes utterances that instruct, unsettle, or transform the reader’s relation to that world. In this model, the first work provides a mythic horizon, while the second examines how a voice can be transmitted and remain operative within that horizon. The relationship resembles the distinction between world-building and the transmission of a tradition. A world may be established through myth, but a tradition requires sayings, practices, interpreters, and mechanisms of preservation. The diptych therefore extends the problem of authorship beyond the individual book. Its works are designed to acquire significance through their relation to one another, through the figures they share, and through the archive that presents them as a coherent literary system. That does not mean the diptych is automatically a unified aesthetic success. The relation must be demonstrated through recurrent motifs, transformations of narrative function, and meaningful differences between the two forms. The archive’s declaration of unity is evidence of authorial intention; close reading determines how fully the texts realize it. 11. A critical assessment: where the work succeeds, and where the claims need testing A serious reading should neither accept the work’s self-description uncritically nor dismiss its ambitions because they are unusually explicit. What appears most successful 1. The conjunction of medium and message. Logion 3 gives the problem of textual transmission an economical formulation. The saying is at once a proposition about the reader and a description of the work’s own existence. 2. The black-box parable. Logion 57 makes the archive emotionally and conceptually legible through a contemporary object. The image connects preservation, catastrophe, testimony, and mortality without requiring an extended theoretical exposition. 3. The contrast between brevity and elaboration. The short sayings and longer parables create a useful variation in pace and interpretive density. The collection’s formal range is not reducible to one rhetorical mode. 4. The explicit relation to Thomas. The shared 114-saying structure and the stated concern with Thomas’s final logion make the comparative project structurally consequential rather than merely thematic. 5. The apparatus as part of the literary problem. The concordance, somatic map, ritual, and commentary make the relationship between text and interpretation unusually visible. What requires closer scrutiny 1. The actual quality of the parallels. The number of correspondences is less important than the precision with which individual sayings are transformed. A synoptic concordance should reveal differences as well as similarities. 2. The final logion. The claim of completing Thomas 114 is a major interpretive commitment. Its success depends on the exact wording, the treatment of gender, and the relation between the two endings. 3. The relation between archive and aesthetic experience. Theoretical vocabulary can clarify the work, but it can also encourage readers to treat every feature as evidence of a pre-existing system. Some images may be more powerful in their ambiguity than in any explanatory framework imposed on them. 4. The distinction between a literary canon and historical authority. The work can construct a coherent literary tradition and a deliberate relation to Thomas. That achievement is different from establishing historical continuity with ancient Christianity or acquiring authority within a religious tradition. 5. The distinction between preservation and reception. A work may be indexed, copied, cited, and made retrievable without being deeply read. The virus and archive metaphors are most interesting when they expose this problem rather than imply that transmission guarantees understanding. These reservations do not diminish the work’s conceptual ambitions. They identify the standards by which those ambitions can be assessed. 12. A research program for a full close reading To move from this structural account to a genuinely exhaustive textual analysis, I would build a working concordance with one row for each of Antioch’s 114 logia. The key is to avoid reducing the comparison to a tally of borrowings. Each saying should be analyzed as an individual literary event and as a node in the larger structure. Analytical field Question Text and wording What does the saying actually say, and what is its grammatical structure? Thomas parallel Which Thomas logion, if any, is proposed as its analogue? Transformation What has been retained, omitted, inverted, expanded, or replaced? Rhetorical mode Is it a paradox, aphorism, imperative, dialogue, parable, or declaration? Temporal structure Does it concern a completed act, present state, future event, or recurring process? Embodiment How does it relate speech, body, identity, and inscription? Position What changes because of its location in the sequence? Recurrence Which motifs or terms connect it to other Antioch sayings? Reception Does the apparatus ask the reader to interpret, perform, map, or transmit it? Aesthetic effect What is achieved through rhythm, brevity, image, tone, or ambiguity? The resulting analysis should then be synthesized at four scales. Microformal: syntax, diction, metaphor, sound, and rhetorical action within each saying. Mesostructural: clusters, recurring images, thematic transitions, and relations among adjacent or distant sayings. Macrostructural: opening, ending, numbering, sequencing, and the relation between the collection and Thomas. Paratextual and developmental: the role of the recorder, the apparatus, the Waltian diptych, and the work’s place in Sharks’s wider literary project. This method would make it possible to determine whether the collection’s architecture is predominantly sequential, thematic, recursive, or networked—and how those different organizing principles interact. It would also make possible a more exact aesthetic judgment. A text can have an elaborate conceptual architecture while individual passages vary in their poetic effectiveness. Conversely, a seemingly slight saying may become structurally decisive through its position and recurrence. Neither result should be assumed before the evidence is examined. Conclusion The Gospel of Antioch is most productively understood as a contemporary literary construction that takes the form of an ancient sayings gospel and uses that form to examine the conditions under which literature survives and acts. Its central movement is from the saying as a bearer of wisdom toward the saying as an element in a system of inscription, transmission, and transformation. Logion 3 makes the person both book and living speech. Logion 10 figures literary agency as a process released into the world. Logion 57 turns the archive into a surviving witness. Logion 42 converts reading into an imperative of becoming. Logion 112 compresses the problem of mortality and textual persistence into two words. These are not identical operations, but they converge on a common problem: how can a voice remain active after it has been separated from the person who speaks it? The relation to Thomas gives that problem historical and formal depth. The shared 114-saying structure and the explicit engagement with Thomas’s final logion make Antioch’s act of composition an argument about succession, interpretation, and the possibility of literary continuation. The work does not merely occupy the sayings-gospel form; it uses that form to make the transmission of sayings one of its central subjects. The most important qualification is that the work’s declared architecture must remain open to textual testing. Its apparatus, its self-positioning within a literary canon, and its claim to complete Thomas are invitations to analysis, not substitutes for it. The strongest case for Antioch will come from demonstrating precisely how its individual sayings transform their antecedents, how the transformations accumulate across the sequence, and how the resulting form produces effects that cannot be reduced to its theoretical description. The governing question, then, is not simply whether Antioch can be read as a new Thomas. It is whether its transformation of Thomas produces a distinct and compelling poetics of literary survival. That is where the work’s most consequential aesthetic and formal claims lie.
